unit.title: Perform advanced welding using oxyacetylene welding process (OAW)

summary: This Level 3 unit takes oxy-acetylene welding (OAW) beyond routine work. You will plan a job and its gas supply, check and look after the equipment, choose the flame and the method for each metal and position, and weld sheet, plate and small-bore pipe. You will also repair cast iron, braze weld, weld aluminium and hardface, test welds, keep the records, and lead and coach a small team safely.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **advanced oxy-acetylene welding**: planning a job and its gas supply, running and maintaining the equipment, choosing flames and methods, positional and pipe welding, other metals, testing, records, and leading others.

Oxy-acetylene is slower than arc welding on thick steel, and it spreads heat more widely. It is still the right tool for many Jamaican jobs: it needs **no electricity**, the set goes on a trolley or the back of a pickup, and it gives fine control on thin sheet and small pipe. The same outfit heats, bends, straightens, braze welds, hardfaces and (with a cutting attachment) cuts. On a hillside farm, a fishing beach or a building with no supply yet, it is often the only practical way to weld.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees and welders who already gas weld flat work safely and now plan the work, set the standard, check other people's welds and write the reports.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at Level 3
rows: Plan the job and the gas supply
Read the procedure, choose the nozzle from the maker's chart, work out the gas needed and how many cylinders, plan transport and set-up.
Work safely and lead safe work
Control fire, explosion, flashback, fume and confined-space risks; deal with leaks, flashbacks and hot cylinders; brief the team.
Run and maintain the equipment
Know how regulators, arrestors, check valves and torch types work; inspect outfits on a programme and keep the log.
Choose and set the flame
Set neutral, carburising or oxidising flames to suit the metal and the process, and read what a faulty flame is telling you.
Weld steel in position
Use the leftward and rightward methods; weld sheet and plate in the horizontal, vertical and overhead positions.
Weld small-bore pipe
Prepare, tack and weld pipe rolled and fixed (1G, 2G, 5G, 6G), make sound tie-ins and branch joints.
Join and repair other metals
Fusion weld cast iron, braze weld, gas weld aluminium and hardface worn parts.
Control distortion
Plan tacking and sequence, and correct buckling by flame straightening.
Test, report and lead
Inspect by eye, run bend, nick-break and macro tests, name defects and causes, keep records, coach trainees and report incidents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on gas supply, safety, equipment, flames, methods, pipe, cast iron, braze welding, aluminium, hardfacing, testing, maintenance and supervision.

A **written paper**: short answers with exact trade terms (for example porous mass, borax, outer envelope, suck-back, firebrick) and calculations; and longer answers that explain a plan, a method or a test.

**Group practical tasks**: a written job plan, leak-tested outfits, butt welds in sheet in the horizontal (2G) and overhead (4G) positions with face and root bend tests, and a small pipe assembly with fixed-position joints, a braze-welded branch, a nick-break test and a job report.

blocks.note: At Level 3 the assessor wants your **reasons**: why this nozzle, why this flame, why this order of work. Learn the "why" in each section, not only the steps.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning the job and the gas supply

blocks.p: Every advanced job starts with a plan. A good plan saves gas, time and rework, and it is where most accidents are prevented.

blocks.h: When oxy-acetylene is the right choice

head: Point
Oxy-acetylene (OAW)

rows: Power

Carrying to site
Cylinders on a trolley or a vehicle
Machine, leads and often a generator

Easy to control the pool and the root

Heating, bending, straightening, braze welding, hardfacing, cutting

ul: The **procedure** (a welding procedure specification, WPS, or the Centre's job sheet): metal, thickness, joint, preparation and positions.
The **nozzle size and pressures** from the maker's chart, the filler rod and any flux, the flame setting and the method (leftward or rightward).
The **order of work**: tacking, the welding sequence, and how distortion will be controlled.
The **gas needed** and the number of cylinders, including any manifold.
The **equipment list**: regulators, arrestors, check valves, hoses, torch, nozzles, tip cleaners, spark lighter, clamps, firebricks, tools, PPE, extinguisher.
**People and roles**: who sets up, who welds which joint, who inspects, who keeps the fire watch.
**Hazards and controls**: fire, fume, confined spaces, overhead work, hot-work permits.
**Inspection and tests**, and the records to be filled in.

blocks.note: The procedure sets the nozzle size, rod, flame and method because they were proved together. If a welder wants to change one (for example a bigger nozzle "to go faster"), he asks first. A change may need approval and a new trial weld.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The maker's nozzle chart gives the pressure to set and the **consumption** of each gas in litres per hour (L/h). With an equal-pressure torch and a neutral flame, the two gases are used in roughly equal amounts (oxygen slightly more).

head: Nozzle (British-style number)
Typical steel thickness
Approximate use of each gas
rows: About 1.2 mm
About 57 L/h
About 2 mm
About 86 L/h
About 2.5 mm
About 140 L/h
About 3 mm
About 200 L/h
About 4 mm
About 280 L/h
About 5 mm
About 370 L/h
About 6.5 mm
About 520 L/h

blocks.note: On many British-style charts the nozzle number is roughly the gas used in cubic feet per hour (1 cubic foot is about 28 litres). Other makers number their tips differently. These are typical figures only: **always use the chart for your own torch**, and follow the maker's instructions and your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A job uses a nozzle that burns about 200 L/h of acetylene, for about 3½ hours of flame time. Acetylene needed = 200 × 3.5 = **700 L**. Add a margin (often 10–20 %) for lighting up, purging and heating. Oxygen will be a little more.

blocks.h: How fast acetylene may be drawn

blocks.p: Acetylene cannot be stored as a compressed gas on its own: it can break down violently. So the cylinder is packed with a **porous mass** soaked with **acetone**, and the acetylene dissolves in the acetone, rather as gas dissolves in a soft drink. When gas is taken out too fast, acetone comes out with it. Acetone in the gas spoils the flame (it often shows a purplish tinge), weakens the weld, and damages regulators, hoses and arrestors. The cylinder also chills as gas leaves it fast.

ul: Never draw acetylene faster than the **supplier's limit**. A common figure for continuous work is **one-seventh of the contents per hour**; some suppliers give a different fraction. Use your supplier's figure.
Always use an acetylene cylinder **upright**, so the acetone stays at the bottom. If it has been lying down, stand it upright for the time the supplier says before use.
When a big nozzle or a heating torch needs more gas than one cylinder may give, join **two or more cylinders on a proper manifold** with the fittings and arrestors the supplier specifies.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A cylinder holds about 7 000 L. One-seventh is 1 000 L per hour. A heating nozzle needs 2 500 L/h. 2 500 ÷ 1 000 = 2.5, so **three** cylinders are needed: always round up, because two would be overdrawn.

blocks.note: Never warm a cylinder, lay it on its side, or open the valve wider to get more gas. These do not make the cylinder safe to overdraw; they make things worse.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Carry cylinders **upright and secured** in an open or well-ventilated vehicle, with the valves shut, the regulators off and the caps on. Never in a closed car boot.
On site, stand them upright and chained or strapped on firm, level ground, in the shade, away from the work, drains and pits.
Store full and empty cylinders **apart and labelled**, so crews take full ones and the stock is easy to check. Store oxygen apart from fuel gases, as the supplier and the Centre's rules say.
Keep stores ventilated, dry, secure and free of oil, rags and rubbish. Chain cylinders so they cannot fall in a storm or be knocked over.

blocks.note: Jamaica's sun heats a cylinder in a truck bed or on a roof quickly, and hot cylinders build up pressure. Park in the shade, cover the load from the sun and unload promptly. Before a trip to a rural site, check the supplier's depot hours: you may not be able to get more gas that day.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Safety on advanced and site work

blocks.p: Advanced work brings bigger nozzles, positional and overhead welding, fluxes, coated metals and site jobs. As the leader you plan the controls and check that others use them.

head: Hazard
Why it matters
Controls
rows: Fire and explosion
Acetylene ignites very easily and burns over a very wide range of mixtures with air (from about 2.5 % to over 80 %). A small leak in a pit, tank or closed room can explode.
Leak test every joint with leak-detection fluid
Cylinders outside confined spaces
Burnables cleared or covered; extinguisher at hand
Acetylene never used above about 1 bar (15 psi)
Oxygen enrichment
Extra oxygen makes clothing, hair and oily rags burst into flame. Oil or grease with oxygen under pressure can ignite on its own.
Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothes or to freshen the air
No oil or grease on oxygen fittings
Shut the torch when not in use
Backfire and flashback
The flame can snap back into the nozzle, burn inside the torch, or travel back up the hoses towards the cylinders.
Flashback arrestors and check valves fitted and in date
Correct pressures for the nozzle
Nozzle kept clean and off the pool
Burns and falling metal
Overhead and positional work drops molten metal and hot slag.
Flame-resistant cap, collar buttoned, sleeves down, leather jacket or sleeves
Stand to the side, not under the joint
Fumes
Zinc, lead paint, cadmium plating, brass rods and fluxes all give harmful fumes.
Extraction or good ventilation
Coatings removed or controlled
Respirator where the risk assessment says
Glare
The flame and the glowing pool are bright; fluxes can flare.
Gas welding goggles or shield of about shade 4–6 (darker for big nozzles)
An arc helmet's shade 10–13 hides the pool

head: Event
What you see and hear
What to do
rows: Backfire
A loud pop; the flame goes out or relights. Common causes: the nozzle touching or held in the pool, an overheated or dirty nozzle, pressures too low for the nozzle, a loose nozzle.
Shut the torch, find the cause, cool and clean the nozzle, check the pressures, then relight.
Sustained backfire
The flame burns inside the torch with a squeal or hiss; sparks or smoke come from the nozzle; the torch neck gets hot.
Close the torch **oxygen** valve at once, then the acetylene; close both cylinder valves; let the torch cool; do not use it until it has been checked.
Flashback
The flame travels back through the mixer into the hoses, perhaps towards the regulators and cylinders. A hose may burn or burst.
Close the cylinder valves if it is safe; check the cylinders for heat; replace or test the arrestors, hoses and torch before any reuse; report it.

blocks.h: If an acetylene cylinder gets hot

blocks.p: Heat from a flashback or a fire can start acetylene breaking down **inside** the cylinder. The breakdown makes its own heat, so the cylinder can stay hot, or heat up again, and burst hours later. Treat any warm acetylene cylinder as an emergency.

flow: If you can do it safely, close the cylinder valve; do not move the cylinder
Clear everyone from the area and keep them out
Call the fire service (in Jamaica, dial 110) and tell them an acetylene cylinder is involved
Cool the cylinder with a water spray from behind cover, and keep cooling it
The fire service decides when it is safe; tell the gas supplier, who takes the cylinder back
Quarantine the outfit, record the incident and find the cause

blocks.note: Never open the valve "to let the heat out", never carry a warm acetylene cylinder outside, and never put it back into use.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Leak test every joint with leak-detection fluid when the set is assembled, after any change and before each session. Never look for a leak with a flame.
A damaged hose is replaced or repaired by a competent person with proper fittings. Never tape a hose or twist wire round it.

If a cylinder valve leaks and will not seal when closed: if it is safe, move the cylinder upright into the open air, away from flames, drains and people; keep sparks away; put up a warning; call the supplier.
If a regulator's working pressure keeps rising with the torch shut (**creep**), its seat is leaking: take it out of use and tag it.
Keep the **cylinders outside** the space. Take the torch out whenever you stop: a leaking torch inside can fill the space with fuel gas or extra oxygen.
Work only under a permit, with the air tested, forced ventilation (air, never oxygen), a standby person outside and a rescue plan.
Never weld or heat a tank, drum or pipe that has held fuel, oil or chemicals until a competent person has cleaned it and declared it safe.

blocks.h: Fumes from metals, coatings and fluxes

head: Source
Risk
Control
rows: Galvanised (zinc-coated) steel
Zinc fume causes **metal fume fever**: chills, fever and aches some hours later
Remove the coating from the weld area; extraction; respirator if needed
Brass and bronze rods (braze welding)
Zinc fume (white smoke) if the pool is overheated
Slightly oxidising flame; ventilation or extraction
Aluminium and cast iron fluxes
Irritating fumes; residues attack metal and skin
Ventilation; gloves; wash residues off the job
Old paint (may contain lead) and plated parts (may contain cadmium)
Serious poisoning
Strip coatings first; ask your instructor; never weld plated parts without special controls
Large flames in closed spaces
The flame uses up oxygen and makes nitrogen oxides
Forced ventilation; air testing

blocks.note: In the dry months, grass, cane trash and bush burn easily. On farms and yards, clear a wide area, wet it down where you can, keep water and an extinguisher ready, and keep a fire watch after you finish.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Equipment: how it works and how to keep it safe

head: Point
Oxygen
Acetylene
rows: How the gas is held
Compressed gas at very high pressure (often around 200 bar when full)
Dissolved in acetone in a porous mass, at a much lower pressure
Position
Upright and secured
Always upright and secured
Outlet thread
Right-hand
Left-hand; nuts often notched
Special dangers
Makes things burn fiercely; never near oil or grease
Unstable if overheated or overdrawn; never through copper pipe
Identification
Read the label: colours differ between suppliers
Read the label: colours differ between suppliers

blocks.note: Acetylene reacts with copper (and with silver) to form explosive compounds. Fittings are made of approved brass, never copper pipe. Use only fittings made for acetylene.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A regulator drops the cylinder pressure to a steady working pressure. The **contents gauge** shows the cylinder pressure; the **working (outlet) gauge** shows what goes to the torch.

head: Type
How it works
Best for
rows: Single-stage
Drops the pressure in one step. As the cylinder empties, the working pressure drifts and must be reset.
Short jobs and general bench work
Two-stage
Drops the pressure in two steps. The working pressure stays steadier as the cylinder empties.
Long runs, heating and pipe work where a steady flame matters

ul: Wind the adjusting screw **out** before you open the cylinder valve, then open the valve slowly, standing to one side of the regulator.
Open an acetylene cylinder valve only as far as the supplier says (often no more than about one and a half turns) and leave the key on it, so it can be shut quickly.
Never oil a regulator. If a gauge is broken, or the needle does not return to zero, tag the regulator out of use.
**Creep** (working pressure rising with the torch shut) means a leaking seat: take it out of use, tag it and have it repaired or replaced.

head: Device
Where it goes
What it does
Care
rows: Flashback arrestor
At the regulator outlet, one for each gas
Stops a flame front reaching the regulator and cylinder; most also contain a non-return valve and some a cut-off that shuts if they get hot
Tested as the maker says (often yearly)
Replaced after a flashback unless the maker says it can be reset
Replaced at the age the maker gives
Check valve (non-return valve)
At the torch inlets
Stops gas flowing backwards into the other hose, where a mixture could form
Checked with the arrestors; replaced if it sticks or leaks

head: Torch type
How the gases are fed
Used with
rows: Equal-pressure (balanced, high-pressure) torch
Both gases arrive at about the same low pressure and are mixed in the **mixer** (mixing chamber)
Cylinder acetylene: the usual torch in Jamaican workshops
Injector (low-pressure) torch
A jet of oxygen at higher pressure draws the acetylene in through an injector
Low-pressure acetylene supplies, and some heating work

blocks.p: Each nozzle size works within a pressure range. To get more heat, fit a **bigger nozzle**. Turning the pressure up on a small nozzle makes a harsh, noisy, fast flame that blows the pool about, oxidises the weld and spatters. Too little pressure on a big nozzle makes a soft flame that pops, backfires and overheats the nozzle.

ul: Clean nozzle holes only with the **right-size tip cleaner**, straight in and out. A drill bit or a piece of wire enlarges or scores the hole and spoils the flame.
Keep the nozzle face flat and clean, and the nozzle seat undamaged. Tighten nozzles by hand or as the maker says.
Store nozzles in a case, not loose in a toolbox.
Acetylene hose is red; oxygen hose is blue in British and European practice and green in American practice. Know which your workshop uses.
Check for cuts, burns, cracks and perishing. Jamaican sun hardens and cracks rubber, so keep hoses coiled in the shade.
Keep hoses out of the path of sparks and slag, off hot metal, and out of walkways and doorways.
Fittings are made up properly by a competent person. Never repair a hose with tape.

blocks.h: An inspection programme for the outfits

blocks.p: Give each outfit a number and a log book or card. Checks are done at set times, and every check and repair is written down: the date, who checked, what was found and what was done.

head: When
By whom
What
rows: Before every use
The user
Cylinders upright and chained
Regulators and gauges undamaged
Arrestors and check valves fitted
Hoses sound; fittings tight and free of oil
Nozzle clean and right size
Leak test passed
At set times (for example monthly)
A competent person
Regulators tested for creep
Arrestors and check valves tested as the maker says
Hoses replaced if worn or old
Torch valves and seals checked
After any flashback, fire, fall or damage
A competent person
Arrestors replaced or tested
Hoses replaced
Regulator and torch checked before reuse
At the maker's service dates
The maker or a service agent
Regulators and arrestors serviced or replaced at the age the maker gives

blocks.note: Any faulty item is tagged DO NOT USE, taken out of service and reported. The log shows the Centre's equipment is safe, and it shows up repeat faults, such as one regulator that keeps creeping.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Equal volumes of oxygen and acetylene from the torch burn in two stages. The first burns at the **inner cone**; just beyond its tip is the hottest point, about **3 100–3 200 °C**. The rest of the gas burns with oxygen from the air in the larger, pale **outer envelope**, which also shields the pool from the air.

head: Flame
How it looks
Gas mix
Used for
Effect on mild steel
rows: Neutral
Clear, rounded inner cone; no feather; quiet
Equal oxygen and acetylene
Mild steel, steel pipe, cast iron fusion welding, copper, flame straightening
Clean, sound weld
Carburising (reducing)
A white **feather** round the inner cone; written 2X or 3X when the feather is two or three times the cone's length
Extra acetylene
Hardfacing (often 3X); aluminium (very slightly)
Adds carbon: hard, brittle weld
Oxidising
Short, pointed, purplish inner cone; harsh hiss
Extra oxygen
Braze welding with brass or bronze rods (slightly)
Burns the metal: sparks, a foamy pool and a porous, brittle weld

blocks.p: A flame of **acetylene alone** (no oxygen) is yellow and smoky and drops black flakes of **soot** (carbon). It is only the first moment of lighting up.

blocks.h: Choosing the flame for the job

head: Job
Flame
Why
rows: Mild steel sheet, plate and pipe
Neutral
Adds nothing to the steel and takes nothing away
Cast iron fusion welding
Neutral (some procedures allow it very slightly carburising)
Keeps the carbon and silicon in the iron and avoids oxides
Aluminium
Neutral or very slightly carburising
Avoids making more oxide on a metal that oxidises easily
Braze welding steel or cast iron with a brass rod
Slightly oxidising
A thin oxide film on the pool stops the zinc boiling off as fume and porosity
Hardfacing with a cobalt-chromium type rod
Carburising (often 3X)
The surface just melts in a thin film (it **sweats**) so the alloy wets it without deep melting
Flame straightening
Neutral, small nozzle
Quick, small spot heats

flow: Check the outfit and leak test it; wind the regulator screws out
Open the cylinder valves slowly; set each working pressure from the chart while purging that hose, one gas at a time
Open the acetylene torch valve a little and light it with a spark lighter, never a match or cigarette lighter
Open the acetylene until the flame stops smoking and sits on the nozzle without lifting off
Open the oxygen slowly until the feather just disappears: a neutral flame
Adjust to carburising or oxidising if the job needs it, starting from neutral
To shut down: close the torch valves in the order the maker and the Centre give (commonly acetylene first), close the cylinder valves, drain each hose, then wind the screws out

head: What you see
Likely cause
What to do
rows: Large, sooty, roaring flame on lighting

Shut down; set the chart pressure; relight
Flame lifts or blows off the nozzle
Pressure too high for the nozzle
Lower the pressure, or fit a bigger nozzle
Popping and backfires
Pressure too low, nozzle dirty, overheated or held too close
Correct pressure; cool and clean the nozzle; hold it off the pool
Flame splits or points to one side
Dirty or damaged nozzle hole
Clean with the right tip cleaner, or replace the nozzle
Purplish tinge; cylinder cold
Acetylene drawn too fast, bringing acetone
Stop; add cylinders on a manifold or use a smaller nozzle
Neutral flame drifts as the nozzle heats
Normal change as the torch warms
Re-check and re-set during the job

blocks.note: To read 2X and 3X, first set a neutral flame, then open the acetylene a little until the feather is twice or three times as long as the inner cone. Practise on scrap until you can judge it by eye.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Point
Leftward (forehand)
Rightward (backhand)
rows: Direction (right-handed welder)
Right to left
Left to right
Filler rod
Held **ahead** of the flame and dipped into the front of the pool
Held **behind** the flame, over the weld just made
Movement
The torch weaves gently side to side; the rod is dipped in and out
The torch moves straight along; the rod moves in small loops in the pool
Typical thickness
Steel up to about 5 mm
Steel over about 5 mm
Edge preparation
Square edges on thin sheet; a wide V (often about 80°) on thicker sheet
A narrower V (about 60°), or square edges with a gap on some thicknesses, as the procedure says
Strong points
Easy pool control on thin sheet
Better view of the root, less filler and gas, faster, less distortion; the flame keeps the weld hot behind the pool
Weak points on thick plate
Needs a wide V, so more rod, more gas and poor fusion at the root
Harder to control on thin sheet

blocks.p: Typical torch angles are about 60–70° to the work for leftward and about 40–50° for rightward, with the rod at about 30–40°. Keep the tip of the inner cone **2–3 mm** off the pool. Follow the angles your instructor and the procedure give.

blocks.note: A good rule for choosing the rod size: about half the plate thickness for leftward work on thin sheet, and the size the procedure gives for thicker plate. A rod that is too big chills the pool and gives a high, narrow bead with poor fusion at the edges.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Position
The problem
How to control it
rows: Horizontal butt (2G): plates upright, weld runs sideways
The pool sags onto the lower plate, leaving undercut on the top edge
Bevel the top plate more than the bottom one, so the bottom edge forms a ledge that holds the pool
Point the flame slightly upward
Add rod to the top edge; keep the pool small
Vertical (3G): weld runs upward
The pool runs down
Weld upward with the flame pointing up the joint
Keep a small pool; add rod at the top of the pool
Use the angle and travel speed to control heat
Overhead (4G)
The pool drips and falls
Smaller pool and slightly less heat (as the procedure allows)
Add rod quickly and often; surface tension holds a small pool
Stand to the side; cap, collar and sleeves done up

blocks.p: In every position, control the heat with the **flame angle and the travel speed**, not by turning the pressures outside the chart.

The flame heats a wide band slowly. The hot metal expands, but the cold metal round it holds it in, so it is squeezed and thickens. When it cools it shrinks and pulls the job out of shape. On a long leftward seam in sheet, the edges ahead of the weld also close up or open out as the heat moves along.

ul: Tack closely and evenly, and plan the order of tacking and welding.
Set the gap a little wider at the far end of a long sheet seam (a tapered gap), or wedge it, so it does not close up.
Clamp the work to a flat table or jig, and use chill bars beside the joint on thin sheet.
Weld in a balanced order, or in short back-step lengths, and avoid over-welding.

blocks.p: Flame straightening uses shrinkage on purpose: a small spot heated quickly on the high side shrinks as it cools and pulls the metal back.

flow: Find the high spots, or the long (convex) side of the bend, with a straight edge
Fit a small nozzle and set a neutral flame
Heat one small spot quickly to a dull red, without melting it (for mild steel, no hotter than a dull red)
Let it cool (in air, or with a damp cloth only if the steel and the supervisor allow)
Work from the edge of the buckle in towards the middle, one spot at a time
Check with the straight edge after each few spots; stop as soon as it is flat

blocks.note: Too much heat, or too many spots in one place, makes the buckle worse. Never flame straighten heat-treated or high-strength steels beyond the limit their maker gives, and only straighten when the supervisor directs.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Gas welding suits **small-bore steel pipe** (often up to about 50–75 mm outside diameter): water and irrigation lines, air lines, handrails and tube frames. The root can be watched and controlled closely.

head: Position
Pipe axis
How the weld runs
rows: 1G (rolled)
Horizontal; the pipe is turned as you weld
Always in the flat, at the top of the pipe: the easiest position, used whenever a small assembly can be rolled
2G
Vertical (upright)
Horizontally round the pipe
5G
Horizontal and fixed
Flat at the top, vertical up the sides, overhead at the bottom
6G
At about 45° and fixed
Through every position: the hardest test

flow: Cut the ends square and remove the burrs
Bevel the ends as the procedure gives (thin-wall pipe may be square edged)
Clean inside and out to bright metal for about 25 mm back
Line the pipes up straight, for example in angle iron or V-blocks, with an even gap all round
Tack in three or four evenly spaced places and check the alignment again
Clean the tacks and make sure the gap has not closed

ul: Weld in **two halves**. Start each half just past the bottom centre and work **upward** to just past the top, so the second half overlaps the first at both ends.
Keep the flame at the same angle to the pipe surface as you go round: your wrist and body move, the angle to the pipe does not.
Keep the pool **small at the bottom** (the overhead part). Too big and hot a pool there sags back and leaves the root sunk inside the bore.
Change your stance before you run out of reach, not in the middle of the pool.

blocks.p: Where the weld meets its own start, take it a little past (often 10–15 mm). Melt the start fully so there is no crater, cold lap or gap. At a restart, re-melt the end of the last run before adding rod.

head: Fault
What it is
Usual causes
Cure
rows: Suck-back (root concavity)
The root inside the pipe has sunk back, leaving a hollow
Too much heat or too big a pool in the overhead part; gap too wide
Smaller pool and less heat at the bottom; correct gap
Excess penetration (icicles)
Weld metal hanging inside the bore
Too much heat; travel too slow; gap too wide
Less heat, faster travel, correct gap
Lack of root penetration
The root has not fused right through
Too little heat; gap too small; root face too big
Correct heat and gap
Misalignment (high-low)
One pipe wall sits higher than the other
Poor line-up before tacking
Align with V-blocks or clamps; check before tacking

head: Type
How it is made
Points to watch
rows: Set-on branch
The branch end is shaped (saddled) to sit on the outside of the main pipe, over a hole
Cut the saddle to a template; get fusion into the main pipe all round
Set-in branch
The branch passes through a hole into the main pipe
Fit the hole closely; weld round the outside of the main pipe

blocks.p: The main pipe is usually heavier, so it draws heat away faster. **Aim more of the flame at the main pipe** and let the pool wash onto the branch, or the weld fuses into the thin branch but sits cold on the main.

blocks.note: Galvanised water pipe gives zinc fume. Remove the coating from the weld area and use extraction, or braze weld if the procedure allows, and repair the coating afterwards.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Cast iron, braze welding, aluminium and hardfacing

blocks.p: Grey cast iron contains a lot of **carbon** (often about 2–4 %), much of it as flakes of graphite. That makes it easy to cast and machine but **brittle**: it will not stretch, so uneven heating or cooling cracks it. A clean break is dull grey; filings and chips are grey and crumbly.

head: Point
Fusion welding
Braze welding
rows: Filler and flux
Cast iron rod with cast iron flux
Brass (bronze) rod with a borax-type flux
Is the casting melted?
Yes: the edges melt into the pool
No: the casting is heated only to tinning heat
Preheat
Whole casting, slowly and evenly, to the temperature the procedure gives (often a dull red)
Less; often local, as the procedure gives
Risk of cracking and distortion
Higher
Lower, because less heat goes in
Colour of the repair
Matches the casting
Yellow, does not match
Hot service
Suitable
Not suitable: the bronze loses strength when hot
Good for
Parts that run hot or must match: manifolds, some machine parts
Brackets, housings and covers at normal temperatures

blocks.h: Fusion welding a casting: key points

ul: Clean off oil and paint, find both ends of the crack (dye penetrant helps) and drill a small **stop hole** at each end so the crack cannot run.
Grind or chip the crack out into a V down to sound metal.

Preheat the **whole** casting slowly and evenly: a furnace, a charcoal fire or a heating torch. Heating only round the crack makes one part grow while the rest stays cold, and the casting cracks again.
Weld with a neutral flame, keeping the pool fluid and working the flux in to float out oxides. Keep the casting hot throughout.
Reheat evenly at the end, then cool **very slowly**, covered in dry sand, ash or an insulating blanket. Never cool it with water or a breeze.
When cold, check for cracks by eye and with dye penetrant.

blocks.p: Braze welding builds up a joint with a **brass** rod (an alloy of copper and zinc, called "bronze" in the trade) that melts at about 870–900 °C. The parent metal is not melted. Unlike capillary brazing, the filler is laid in a groove or fillet like a weld.

flow: Clean the joint to bright metal and fit it; bevel thicker parts so the bronze can fill and grip a large area
Set a slightly oxidising flame
Heat the steel or iron to a dull red: the **tinning** heat
Dip the hot rod in flux (or use a flux-coated rod) and touch it on: at the right heat the bronze flows and wets the surface in a thin film
Build up the joint, moving steadily and keeping the surface at tinning heat

head: What you see
What it means
What to do
rows: White smoke from the pool
Zinc boiling off: too hot, or the flame not oxidising enough
Less heat; slightly oxidising flame; ventilation
Bronze balls up and will not spread
Surface too cold, dirty or short of flux
More heat; clean; more flux
Bronze runs off and the steel starts to melt
Too hot
Pull the flame back; travel faster

blocks.p: Choose braze welding for cast iron that does not run hot, galvanised steel (less of the coating is burnt off than in fusion welding), joining unlike metals (steel to cast iron or copper), and thin parts that would distort. Do not use it for parts that work hot (above roughly 250 °C) or need the full strength of steel.

ul: Aluminium melts at about 660 °C, but its tough **oxide skin** melts only above 2 000 °C. A **flux** is painted on the joint and the rod to dissolve the oxide; without it the metal will not fuse.
It shows **no colour** before it melts. Watch for the surface to look **wet and shiny**, then start the pool.
It carries heat away several times faster than steel. It needs a lot of heat to start, then the whole part heats up and the pool grows quickly: **travel faster as you go**.
Near its melting point it has almost no strength and can collapse without warning, so support it on a backing plate or **firebrick**.
Use a neutral or very slightly carburising flame, the leftward method and an aluminium rod that suits the alloy, as the procedure gives.
Wash **all** the flux off afterwards with hot water and a brush: left on, it draws in moisture and corrodes the metal. Ventilate: the flux fumes irritate.

blocks.note: Some aluminium alloys are heat treated for strength, and gas welding softens them. Check the procedure before welding a structural or load-bearing aluminium part.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Hardfacing** lays a hard, wear-resistant alloy on parts that rub on soil, stone or other parts, so they last longer and cost less than new ones. In Jamaica it is used on plough shares, cultivator tines, harrow discs, quarry tools, mixer paddles and cane-cutting parts.

ul: Clean the part to bright metal and grind off cracked or badly worn metal.
Preheat if the rod maker says, to stop cracking.
Use a **carburising flame** (often 3X). The steel surface just **sweats** (a thin wet film) without a deep pool.
Melt the rod onto the sweating surface so it wets and spreads; build up thin, even layers to the shape needed.
Keep the base metal from melting deeply: mixing steel into the hard alloy (**dilution**) makes the surface softer and shortens its life.
Cool slowly as the maker says, inspect for cracks and even thickness, and record the rod used and the area covered.

sections.title: Testing, faults, records and leading the team

blocks.p: Every weld is inspected visually before any other test: size and profile, even ripples, undercut, overlap, cracks, surface porosity, root penetration where it can be seen, and the job's alignment and sizes.

head: Test
How it is done
What it shows
rows: Nick-break
A saw cut is made in each edge of the weld and the strip is broken through the weld
Gas holes, oxide, lack of fusion and poor penetration on the broken face
Face bend
A strip across the weld is bent with the **face** on the outside of the bend
Lack of fusion and defects near the face
Root bend
Bent with the **root** on the outside
Lack of root fusion or penetration
Macro-etch
The weld is cut across, smoothed and etched with the etchant the Centre approves
The weld's shape, fusion, penetration and heat-affected zone
Dye penetrant
Coloured dye soaks into surface cracks; a developer draws it out
Surface cracks, for example after a cast iron repair
Pressure or leak test
Pipework filled and pressurised as the specification says
Leaks in pipe joints

ul: Mark every test piece with the welder's number before cutting.
Cut strips from the places the test procedure gives, away from starts and stops.
**Dress the cap and root flush** and round the edges, so the shape of the weld or a notch does not cause a false fail.
Bend round a former of the size the procedure gives; record any opening, its size and position, against the acceptance limits.

head: Fault
Likely causes
Cure
rows: Burnt, porous weld; sparks; foamy pool
Oxidising flame; too much heat
Neutral flame; correct nozzle
Hard, brittle weld
Carburising flame on steel
Neutral flame
High, narrow bead with poor edge fusion
Nozzle too small, rod too big, or too much rod for the heat
Correct nozzle and rod; melt the edges before adding rod
Burn-through near the end of each run
Heat builds up ahead of the weld
Flatten the flame angle and travel faster towards the end
Undercut
Wrong flame angle; pool too hot; too little rod at the edges
Correct angle; add rod at the edges
Lack of fusion (cold lap)
Rod melted by the flame and dropped on cold metal; travel too fast
Melt into the pool; slow down; more heat
Porosity
Dirty metal; oxidising flame; zinc or paint
Clean to bright metal; neutral flame; remove coatings
Cracks
Fast cooling; uneven heating of cast iron; restraint
Preheat; slow cooling; correct sequence

blocks.note: A **crack** is the most serious fault and is always rejected. It is ground out, the groove is checked to prove the crack has gone, and it is re-welded to the procedure.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Record
What it holds
rows: Outfit log
Every inspection, test and repair of each numbered outfit
Gas log
Cylinders received, used and returned; gas used on each job
Weld and test record
Welder, joint, procedure, settings, test results against the limits
Job report
What was done, gas and materials used, faults found, what would be changed
Incident report (for example a flashback)
What happened, when and where, who was involved, the likely cause, equipment checked or replaced, actions to stop it happening again

ul: **Brief** the team before work: the job, the procedure, the hazards and controls, who does what, and the checks.
Before anyone lights up, check every station: arrestors, check valves, hoses, regulators, secured cylinders, leak test, extinguisher.
Watch trainees light up and set flames. If a set-up is wrong, **stop it** first, then show the right way (the chart pressures and the lighting order) and let them practise.
Coach from the fault: name it, find the cause, show the cure, then check the next weld.
Never let "faster" replace the procedure. Report and record near misses as well as accidents.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can say when oxy-acetylene is the best process for a job, and when it is not.
I can write a job plan covering the procedure, nozzle, flame, method, sequence, gas, equipment, people, hazards and tests.
I can work out gas used, cylinder hours, safe withdrawal rates and the number of cylinders on a manifold.
I can explain why acetylene must be drawn slowly and used upright, and how cylinders are carried and stored.
I can deal with backfire, sustained backfire, flashback, leaks and a hot acetylene cylinder.
I can control the risks of confined spaces, oxygen enrichment, overhead work and fumes from coatings and fluxes.
I can explain single- and two-stage regulators, creep, arrestors, check valves and torch types.
I can run an inspection programme for gas outfits and keep its log.
I can set neutral, carburising and oxidising flames and choose the right one for each job.
I can choose between leftward and rightward welding and weld in the 2G, 3G and 4G positions.
I can control distortion and straighten a buckled panel with spot heats.
I can prepare, tack and weld small-bore pipe in fixed positions, with sound tie-ins and branch joints.
I can repair cast iron by fusion welding or braze welding and say which suits a job.
I can gas weld aluminium and hardface a worn part.
I can run visual, bend, nick-break and macro tests and name the faults and their causes.
I can brief, supervise and coach a team, and write job and incident reports.

terms: Acetone
The liquid inside an acetylene cylinder in which the acetylene is dissolved
Backfire
The flame snapping back into the nozzle with a pop and going out or relighting
Borax
A white boron compound used as the base of fluxes for braze welding
Braze welding
Building up a joint with a brass (bronze) rod without melting the parent metal
Brass
An alloy of copper and zinc; the usual braze welding rod
Carburising flame
A flame with extra acetylene, showing a white feather round the inner cone
Check valve
A non-return valve at the torch that stops gas flowing back into the other hose
Cracking a valve
Opening a cylinder valve briefly and closing it, to blow out dust before the regulator is fitted
Creep
A regulator's working pressure rising with the torch shut, from a leaking seat
Dilution
Parent metal mixing into the weld or hardfacing
Equal-pressure torch
A torch fed with both gases at about the same pressure, mixed in the mixer
Firebrick
A heat-resistant block used to support work on a gas welding bench
Flame straightening
Removing distortion with small, quick spot heats that shrink as they cool
Flashback
The flame travelling back through the torch into the hoses
Flashback arrestor
A device at the regulator outlet that stops a flame front reaching the regulator and cylinder
Hardfacing
Laying a hard, wear-resistant alloy on a part
Inner cone
The bright cone at the nozzle; its tip is the hottest part of the flame
Leftward welding
Welding with the rod ahead of the flame; for thinner steel
Manifold
Pipework joining two or more cylinders to supply one outlet
Mixer
The part of the torch where the oxygen and acetylene are mixed
Neutral flame
Equal oxygen and acetylene; clear inner cone, no feather
Nick-break test
Breaking a weld strip through saw cuts to see inside the weld
Outer envelope
The pale outer part of the flame that surrounds the inner cone and shields the pool
Oxidising flame
A flame with extra oxygen; short, pointed inner cone
Porous mass
The filling inside an acetylene cylinder that holds the acetone
Rightward welding
Welding with the rod behind the flame; for thicker steel
Set-on and set-in branch
A branch pipe sitting on the main pipe, or passing through a hole into it
Stop hole
A small hole drilled at each end of a crack to stop it running
Suck-back
A pipe root that has sunk back to leave a hollow inside the bore
Sweating
The steel surface just melting in a thin film under a carburising flame
Tie-in
Taking the end of a run past its start so the two fuse fully
Tinning
Bronze flowing and wetting a hot, clean surface in a thin film
Two-stage regulator
A regulator that reduces pressure in two steps for a steadier flame

c1.title: Straightening cane-carrier rails in Frome
c1.text: Kirk-Anthony, a Level 3 welder, leads a two-person team in a sugar factory workshop in Frome, Westmoreland. They must heat and straighten bent steel rails from a cane carrier, using a large heating nozzle that burns about 2 500 litres of acetylene an hour, for about 4 hours. Each acetylene cylinder holds about 7 000 litres, and the supplier's limit is one-seventh of the contents an hour. A factory worker suggests laying one cylinder on its side "so the gas comes out quicker".

c2.title: A squealing torch in Ocho Rios
c2.text: During an evening class at a training centre in Ocho Rios, St Ann, a trainee, Jodian, is welding 3 mm sheet with her nozzle almost buried in the pool. There is a loud pop, then a steady squeal; smoke and sparks come from the nozzle and the torch neck gets hot. Her partner shuts the cylinder valves. Afterwards the acetylene cylinder feels warm near the top. Tavares, the Level 3 trainee leading the bay, must act. The outfit's flashback arrestors are a type that cannot be reset.

c3.title: An irrigation header test in Spaldings
c3.text: At a training centre in Spaldings, Clarendon, Level 3 trainees are gas welding 50 mm steel pipe for an irrigation header. Nadine has welded a joint fixed with the pipe axis horizontal. When it is cut open, the root inside the bottom of the pipe has sunk below the bore, while the root at the top is full and even. Rohan has welded a 25 mm set-on branch onto the 50 mm main: his weld has fused well into the branch but sits on the main pipe without melting into it.

c4.title: A cracked manifold in Little London
c4.text: A guest house in Little London, Westmoreland, sends in the cracked cast-iron exhaust manifold from its standby diesel generator. The manifold runs very hot in service. Shanice, the shop's Level 3 welder, finds a 60 mm crack running out from a bolt hole. The owner wants it braze welded "because it is quicker". The same customer has also brought a galvanised steel handrail with a broken joint, which Shanice will braze weld with a brass rod.

c5.title: Farm repairs near Southfield
c5.text: A vegetable farm near Southfield, St Elizabeth, brings two jobs to a small workshop: a set of steel cultivator tines worn thin by the sandy soil, to be hardfaced with a cobalt-chromium type rod, and an aluminium irrigation pipe coupling with a split along its 3 mm wall. Dameon, the Level 3 welder, will hardface the tines himself and coach a trainee, Akeem, on the aluminium coupling.

questions.q: Which set-up lets Kirk-Anthony feed this nozzle without breaking the supplier's limit?
o: Three cylinders joined on a manifold, sharing the load
Two cylinders on a manifold, each run at its full limit
One cylinder with its valve opened as far as it will go
Four cylinders, since each may give only 625 litres an hour
questions.why: Each cylinder may give 7 000 ÷ 7 = 1 000 L an hour. The nozzle needs 2 500 L an hour, which is 2.5 cylinders' worth, so round up to three; two would be overdrawn.

questions.q: Roughly how much acetylene will the 4-hour heating job use, not counting waste?
o: About 625 litres
About 2 500 litres
About 10 000 litres
About 28 000 litres
questions.why: Gas used = rate × time = 2 500 L/h × 4 h = 10 000 L. Three 7 000 L cylinders hold enough; what limits the set-up is the rate of draw, not the contents.

questions.q: What is wrong with the worker's idea of laying a cylinder on its side?
o: Liquid acetone would flow out with the gas towards the regulator and flame
The gas would come out more slowly than it does when the cylinder is upright
It is safe as long as the cylinder is chained so it cannot roll
It would only matter once the cylinder was nearly empty
questions.why: The acetylene is dissolved in acetone inside a porous mass. Upright, the acetone stays at the bottom; on its side, liquid acetone can reach the valve, spoil the flame and damage the regulator, hoses and arrestors.

questions.q: An hour into the job, the flame shows a purplish tinge and the cylinders feel cold. What does this most likely mean?
o: The flame has become oxidising, so the oxygen should be turned down
Gas is being drawn too fast, so acetone is coming out with it
The cylinders are almost empty and need their valves opened further
The rails are drawing heat from the flame, which is normal on thick steel
questions.why: A purplish flame and chilled cylinders are signs of overdrawing. Stop, and either add cylinders to the manifold or use a smaller nozzle, so each cylinder stays within the limit.

questions.q: When the torch began to squeal and smoke, what should have been done first?
o: Close the acetylene torch valve and leave the oxygen running to cool the torch
Close the torch's oxygen valve straight away, then the acetylene valve
Plunge the lit torch into a bucket of water before touching any valve
Pull the hoses off the torch so that no more gas can reach the flame
questions.why: A squeal with smoke and sparks is a sustained backfire: the flame is burning inside the torch. Shutting the oxygen first starves it at once; then shut the acetylene and both cylinder valves, and let the torch cool.

questions.q: Why will the fire service keep cooling the warm acetylene cylinder for a long time, even after it feels cooler?
o: The acetone inside will freeze if the cylinder is cooled too quickly
Water stops the paint on the cylinder from blistering in the heat
The cylinder must be cold before the valve can be opened to empty it
Acetylene inside can keep breaking down and reheat the cylinder
questions.why: Heat can start the acetylene decomposing inside the cylinder, and the breakdown makes its own heat, so it can reheat and burst hours later. The area stays clear and the cylinder is never opened, moved or reused; the supplier takes it back.

questions.q: Before this outfit is used again, what must happen to the flashback arrestors?
o: Nothing, provided the outfit passes a leak test with fluid
They are tapped firmly to free the valves, then refitted
They are taken apart, cleaned and oiled so that they move freely
They are replaced, as this type cannot be reset
questions.why: An arrestor that has stopped a flashback may be damaged inside and no longer protect the cylinder. A non-resettable type is replaced, and the hoses, regulators and torch are checked before reuse. Arrestors are never oiled.

questions.q: What should Tavares coach Jodian to do differently before she welds again?
o: Turn both pressures up so the flame is too strong to pop back
Fit a smaller nozzle and raise the pressure to keep the heat
Light the oxygen first so the flame is neutral from the start
Hold the inner cone tip a few millimetres off the pool
questions.why: Holding the nozzle in the pool blocks the gas, overheats the nozzle and causes backfires. The inner cone should stay about 2–3 mm off the pool, with the chart pressures for the nozzle and a clean, cool nozzle.

questions.q: What most likely caused the sunken root at the bottom of Nadine's pipe?
o: Too much heat and too big a pool in the overhead part
A flame that was slightly carburising all the way round
Too little heat at the top, where she finished the weld
Too many tacks placed round the joint before welding
questions.why: At the bottom of a fixed horizontal pipe the welder is working overhead. A large, hot pool there sags back under gravity and leaves suck-back (root concavity). Keep the pool small at the bottom and check the gap.

questions.q: How should a fixed horizontal (5G) pipe joint be welded with oxy-acetylene?
o: In one run all the way round, starting and ending at the top
In two uphill halves that overlap at the bottom and the top
Downhill from the top on one side, then uphill on the other side
In short runs placed at random to share out the heat evenly
questions.why: Each half is welded upward from just past the bottom centre to just past the top, so the second half overlaps the first at both ends and the tie-ins are fully fused.

questions.q: Why did Rohan's weld fuse into the branch but not into the main pipe, and what should he change?
o: The branch was too thick for the rod; he should use a bigger rod
The flame was far too hot; he should change to a smaller nozzle
The main pipe soaks up heat; he should aim more flame at it
The pipes were too clean; he should leave the mill scale on
questions.why: The larger main pipe soaks up heat faster than the thin branch. Directing more of the flame at the main pipe and letting the pool wash onto the branch gives fusion into both.

questions.q: The assessor wants to see the shape, fusion and penetration of Rohan's branch weld in section. Which test suits this best?
o: A face bend test on a strip cut from the branch
A leak test using soapy water on the outside
A hardness test on the cap of the weld
A macro-etch of a slice cut across the weld
questions.why: A macro-etch shows the cross-section: the weld profile, how far it has fused into each pipe, and the root. A bend strip is hard to cut from a branch, and a leak test shows only whether it leaks.

questions.q: Which repair should Shanice recommend for the manifold?
o: Braze weld it with a brass rod, as the owner asked, then paint it
Fusion weld it with cast iron rod and flux, with full preheat
Weld it cold with mild steel rod to keep the heat in the casting low
Braze weld it and fit a heat shield round it to keep it cooler
questions.why: Braze-welded joints lose strength at high temperature, and a generator manifold runs very hot. Fusion welding with cast iron rod and flux gives a repair that matches the casting and stands the heat.

questions.q: Why must the whole manifold be preheated, and not only the area round the crack?
o: So the flux melts before the filler rod reaches the crack
So that less acetylene is needed for the weld itself
So it expands evenly and the brittle iron does not crack
So that the colour of the repair matches the rest of the casting
questions.why: Cast iron cannot stretch. If one area is hot and the rest cold, the hot part grows and the casting cracks. Even preheat, keeping it hot while welding and very slow cooling stop this.

questions.q: Which flame should Shanice set to braze weld the galvanised handrail, and why?
o: Slightly oxidising, to stop the zinc in the rod boiling off as fume
Neutral, so the steel melts into the bronze as in a fusion weld
Strongly carburising, so the zinc coating is protected from the heat
Strongly oxidising, so it is hot enough to burn off all the zinc
questions.why: A slightly oxidising flame forms a thin oxide film on the bronze pool that holds the zinc in, cutting white zinc fume and porosity. Ventilation or extraction is still needed for the zinc on the rail and in the rod.

questions.q: When Shanice reaches the right heat on the rail, what should she see as she touches the fluxed rod to it?
o: The bronze flowing out thinly over the steel
The steel melting into a bright pool under the flame
The bronze forming round balls that roll off the steel
The flux burning black and smoking on the surface
questions.why: At tinning heat (a dull red on steel) the bronze wets the clean surface in a thin film, as solder does. Balls mean the steel is too cold, dirty or short of flux; a melting pool means it is too hot.

questions.q: Why should Dameon keep the steel from melting deeply under the hardfacing?
o: Steel mixed into the alloy makes the hard surface softer
Deep melting makes the tines too hard to bend back into shape
Shallow melting lets him use a bigger nozzle and finish sooner
Melting the steel deeply would use up too much of the flux
questions.why: This mixing is called dilution. The carburising flame lets the surface just sweat, so the cobalt-chromium alloy wets it with little steel mixed in, and keeps its full hardness and wear resistance.

questions.q: Akeem struggles to start a pool on the aluminium, then a few centimetres later the metal suddenly sags. What should Dameon tell him?
o: Use a strongly oxidising flame so the metal gets hot more quickly
Turn the pressures up on a smaller nozzle to concentrate the heat
It spreads heat fast, so he must speed up as the part heats
Stop adding flux once the pool has started, so it does not cool
questions.why: Aluminium conducts heat away quickly, so it is slow to start; then the whole part heats up and, with no colour change to warn him, it loses strength and sags. He should travel faster as he goes and support the coupling on a firebrick.

questions.q: A trainee uses the oxygen hose to blow dust off his overalls before a break. What is the danger?
o: The cold oxygen can freeze the skin through the cloth
The dust may block the nozzle and cause backfires later
The oxygen will be wasted, and the job may run short of gas
The cloth holds oxygen, so a spark can set it ablaze
questions.why: Oxygen soaks into clothing and stays there for some time. A spark or hot spatter can then make the cloth burst into flame and burn fiercely. Never use oxygen for dusting or for ventilation.

questions.q: A nozzle burns about 370 litres of oxygen an hour. About how many hours of flame will a full 6 800-litre oxygen cylinder give?
o: About 9 hours
About 18 hours
About 25 hours
About 54 hours
questions.why: Hours = contents ÷ rate = 6 800 ÷ 370 ≈ 18.4, so about 18 hours. In practice allow a margin, as some gas is used lighting up, purging and heating.
